papers.title: Dependence-aware aggregation maps shared genetic architecture across cardiovascular traits
papers.abstract: Background Shared genetic effects are pervasive across clinically related cardiovascular diseases and can expose biology that crosses diagnostic boundaries, but correlation between related phenotypes (shared patients, risk factors, overlapping definitions) makes naive cross-trait recurrence hard to interpret because evidence is counted repeatedly. We asked which genes carry coordinated positive association across a complete cardiovascular panel beyond the recurrence expected from trait dependence. Methods We developed the Cross-Trait Aggregation Score (CTAS), a per-gene statistic applied to MAGMA gene-level association across 16 Pan-UK Biobank cardiovascular traits. Panel dependence was estimated as a transformed rank-correlation matrix; each gene's 16-trait profile was decorrelated by ZCA-cor whitening to remove the expected correlation; and CTAS combined the magnitude and effective breadth of positive residual evidence across the whitened coordinates. The statistic was calibrated against an empirical null of 10 simulated profiles, with genome-wide Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate control, after which significant genes were merged into loci and characterised by clinical-family composition, expression colocalisation, comparison with prior multi-trait studies and FinnGen. Results CTAS prioritised 223 genes at 91 loci (q<0.05), with nested sets of 99 genes at 46 loci (q<0.01) and 38 genes at 21 loci (q<0.001); membership was identical across independent null simulations. The loci formed an overlapping multi-family continuum rather than discrete disease classes: 88% spanned at least two clinical families and the fraction spanning four or more increased from 21% to 43% across the nested sets. Expression colocalisation supported 31 of 91 loci (31 of 87 evaluable). Literature convergence with four prior multi-trait studies covered 58 of 91 loci and 17 of the 21 most stringent loci. In FinnGen, the proportion of CTAS genes with external support across at least three of six clinical families of cardiovascular endpoints increased across the nested sets, from 49% at q<0.05 to 57% at q<0.01 and 61% at q<0.001, against 6% of background genes. Conclusions CTAS evaluates a complete correlated trait panel in one calibrated test per gene, discounting the recurrence expected from trait correlation. In cardiovascular disease, it prioritised genes and loci with multi-family, independently supported evidence, providing a focused starting point for mechanistic and translational follow-up.

papers.title: Single-Cell Gene Expression Heritability Informed by Genotype x Cell-Context Interactions
papers.abstract: Most signals from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of complex traits implicate noncoding variants with putative gene regulatory effects. However, currently identified regulatory variants, particularly expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs), explain only a small fraction of GWAS associations. Moreover, GWAS loci are enriched near evolutionarily constrained genes, whereas constrained genes are depleted of detectable eQTLs, suggesting that weak or context-specific regulatory mechanisms may contribute substantially to disease risk but remain poorly captured by existing approaches. Here, we introduce scHINT (single-cell gene expression Heritability estimation with genotype x context INTeraction), a computationally efficient framework for quantifying cell-level expression heritability and context-dependent genetic regulation from large-scale single-cell data. Applying scHINT to human brain single-nucleus RNA-seq data, we found that genotype-by-cell-state heritability was widespread across brain cell types and, on average, exceeded main genetic heritability, indicating that context-dependent genetic effects explain a substantial fraction of heritable expression variation. GxCell-State heritability was enriched among low-frequency variants and constrained genes, and showed stronger enrichment for functional gene sets and disease heritability than main genetic effects. Using a novel GxCell-State TWAS framework, we identified 68% more disease-risk genes and recapitulated rare-variant burden-test gene TREM2, which was missed by state-agnostic TWAS. In blood, we observed the same direction of enrichment for GxCell-State heritability at constrained genes, but weaker than in brain, suggesting that cell-state-dependent regulation at constrained genes may be more prominent in brain. Finally, extending scHINT to perturbation screens revealed substantial perturbation-by-cell-state effects, highlighting broad context dependence in transcriptional responses.

papers.title: Eating disorder phenotypes differ in their genetic relationships with impulsivity facets
papers.abstract: Background. Eating disorders are clinically heterogeneous and characterized by distinct patterns of control over food intake. Anorexia nervosa (AN) is characterized by excessive dietary restraint, whereas binge-eating (BE) is a transdiagnostic behavior defined by loss of control over eating. Understanding the relationship between eating disorders and impulsivity may provide insights into their underlying mechanisms and identify potential targets for prevention and treatment. Methods. We used genome-wide association study data (N=82,707-1,268,116) and genomic structural equation modeling to examine genetic relationships between eating disorder phenotypes (AN, ANRestrictive, ANBinge-Purging, and BE) and impulsivity facets (five UPPS-P, three BIS-11, and delay discounting). We examined whether these relationships persisted after conditioning on the genetic liability for substance use disorders (SUDs) and body mass index (BMI). Results. AN and its subtypes showed negative genetic correlations with delay discounting, the magnitude of this correlation being stronger for ANRestrictive. ANRestrictive also showed negative genetic correlations with sensation seeking and common impulsivity, whereas ANBinge-Purging showed a positive genetic correlation with urgency-specific impulsivity. In contrast, BE showed positive genetic correlations with both common and urgency-specific impulsivity. Several associations remained significant after controlling for SUDs and BMI, including the negative association between AN with delay discounting, the negative associations with AN and ANRestrictive with sensation seeking, and the positive association between BE and urgency-specific impulsivity. Conclusion. These findings reveal complex patterns of genetic overlap between eating disorder phenotypes and impulsivity dimensions. Understanding these phenotype-specific relationships may help explain clinical heterogeneity and inform the development of more targeted prevention and treatment strategies.

papers.title: Long-read sequencing resolves functional CYP2D6 alleles tagged by a cocaine use disorder associated haplotype
papers.abstract: The CYP2D6 locus exhibits extensive allelic diversity and structural complexity, complicating the identification of functional variants underlying genetic associations. We previously identified a four-single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) haplotype (AACG) associated with cocaine use disorder and altered CYP2D6 expression in the brain. To characterize the molecular variation of this haplotype, we performed targeted PacBio long-read sequencing on 19 individuals of European ancestry carrying zero, one, or two copies of AACG. Complementary analyses included human pangenome assemblies, protein structural modeling, splice quantitative trait loci, and SNP-array probe sequences. Long-read sequencing resolved distinct CYP2D6 alleles associated with AACG, including CYP2D6 star 2 and star 4. Four of five individuals lacking AACG carried two canonical reference alleles, whereas nearly all AACG homozygotes carried noncanonical alleles. The star 2 allele contained two missense substitutions (R296C and S486T), while star 4 carried four missense substitutions (P34S, L91M, H94R, and S486T) and a loss-of-function splice-site mutation. Structural comparisons suggested potential substrate-dependent effects on ligand binding, while publicly available transcriptomic data associated AACG variants with altered splice-junction usage across multiple tissues, including brain. Although SNP-array intensity differences initially suggested copy-number variation, long-read sequencing did not support consistent gene dosage differences. Instead, polymorphisms within array probe-binding regions provided a plausible explanation for these signals. These findings demonstrate that a disease-associated SNP haplotype tags functionally distinct CYP2D6 alleles and highlight the importance of haplotype-resolved sequencing for interpreting genetic associations at complex pharmacogenomic loci.

papers.title: Direct RNA sequencing reveals an m6A downregulated on APOEϵ4 RNA in brain from Alzheimer's disease cases and controls
papers.abstract: APOE harbors the strongest common genetic risk factors for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet its disease mechanism remains incompletely understood. Two missense SNPs jointly define the APOE alleles, with rs429358 distinguishing {epsilon}4 from {epsilon}3, but whether other APOE features, such as mRNA modifications, contribute to APOE-associated AD risk is unknown. Here, we performed deep long-read direct RNA sequencing on human frontal cortex from six AD cases and six controls to characterize native mRNA modifications transcriptome-wide and across AD-relevant genes. We evaluated differential nucleotide modifications between cases and controls transcriptome-wide, and we then performed two association tests within APOE: (1) associations between mRNA modifications and rs429358 alleles in five {epsilon}3/{epsilon}4 heterozygotes; and (2) pairwise associations between co-occurring mRNA modifications. We identified four modifications associated with rs429358--all within 15 nucleotides of the SNP. Among them was an N6-methyladenosine (m6A) located at chr19:44,908,679 (OR = 0.53; p = 1.4x10-109)--five nucleotides upstream of rs429358--that was 14.5 percentage points lower on {epsilon}4-derived mRNA (27.7%) compared to {epsilon}3 (42.2%). This directional difference was observed within each individual, supporting a consistent allele-associated modification pattern (p = 4.2x10-5). We also identified 344 associations among 73 APOE modifications, suggesting a potentially complex, coordinated network of mRNA biological signals within APOE, alone. Our findings suggest that mRNA modifications may contribute to APOE-associated risk, though validation in large independent cohorts and functional experiments will be necessary to determine the biological consequences of these associations and their potential relevance to AD pathogenesis. Together, our findings highlight the potential of allele-resolved direct RNA sequencing to characterize genetic associations with RNA modifications at a major AD risk locus.

papers.title: Regional brain-age gaps reveal a shared polygenic architecture and regionally patterned clinical and cell-type associations
papers.abstract: A single brain-age estimate may obscure regional differences in clinical vulnerability. Using voxel-level deep learning, we derived whole-brain and nine regional brain-age gaps (BAGs) spanning cortical, subcortical and cerebellar regions from T1-weighted MRI in 46,254 UK Biobank participants. Genetic correlation estimates in 41,067 participants (rg = 0.56-0.93) exceeded phenotypic correlations across all 45 pairs, yet regional profiles varied across 24 hospital-recorded diagnoses. Oligodendrocyte annotations predominated for whole-brain and cerebellar BAGs, whereas annotations for caudate BAG included astrocyte and vascular classes. In the Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, temporal BAG showed stronger associations with cerebrospinal fluid A{beta}42 and cognition than whole-brain BAG when modelled together. A regional model modestly improved discrimination of observed conversion from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimers disease during available follow-up compared with a whole-brain model. Polygenic scores showed cross-cohort associations with hypertension and osteoporosis. Regional BAGs provide complementary clinical information within a shared polygenic architecture.

papers.title: Genetic analysis of non-familial early-onset Alzheimer's disease patients
papers.abstract: Early-onset Alzheimers disease (EOAD), defined by symptom onset before age 65, can be either familial or sporadic and account for [~]5% of all Alzheimers disease (AD) cases, with only [~]10% showing Mendelian inheritance. In this study, we compare the genetic architecture of four cohorts comprising 87 sporadic EOAD cases, 1,018 late-onset AD (LOAD) cases, 585 non-demented control (TGEN2-AD and TGEN2-ND cohorts), and 3,487 non-demented controls from the AD Sequencing Project (ADSP-CTL). We observed a significant enrichment of the APOE {varepsilon}4 allele in EOAD cohort compared to controls (52.2% vs 20.1%; p = 1.54e-10), although its frequency was lower than in the LOAD cohort (64.5%; p = 0.0298). As expected, APOE {varepsilon}4 was strongly enriched in the LOAD group relative to controls (p = 1.23e-63). Sporadic EOAD genome-wide association (GWAS) analysis and sequence kernel association tests (SKAT) confirmed strong association signals in the APOE locus, including the genes APOE, APOC1, NECTIN2, and TOMM40. AD-related Polygenic Risk Score (PRS) showed that EOAD affected patients carried an intermediate genetic risk (mean PRS = 40.1), significantly lower than LOAD (mean PRS = 57.5; p = 6.7e-05) but higher than controls (mean PRS = 25.1; p = 6.1e-04). Notably, rare variants in autosomal dominant AD genes (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2) and in previously reported EOAD/LOAD modifier genes where not enriched in sporadic EOAD cohort. These results suggest, despite earlier onset, sporadic EOAD is not driven by a higher polygenic burden or rare high-impact variants. Instead, its genetic architecture appears to overlap more closely with LOAD, supporting the hypothesis that EOAD may represent an early and more severe manifestation of LOAD, or a genetically distinct subtype. Unidentified risk factors, such as epigenetic modifications or complex structural variants, may contribute to EOAD genetic risk and warrant further investigation to better elucidate the complex genetic architecture of Alzheimers disease.

papers.title: Scalable cell-state-resolved TWAS identified dynamic autoimmune disease genes along functional programs
papers.abstract: Transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) are widely used to prioritize genes for complex diseases. TWAS typically trains models on expression quantitative disease locus (eQTL) reference data to predict gene expression from genotype, then tests for association between the predicted expression and disease. With the rapid growth of single-cell eQTL data, there is a pressing need for methods that can fully leverage cell-level information. We previously developed TWiST, the first method for TWAS at cell-state resolution. TWiST is powerful, but training its prediction model is computationally expensive. Here we propose Fast-TWiST, an accelerated and scalable version of TWiST that can analyze hundreds of thousands to millions of cells. Fast-TWiST computes donor-level summary statistics that retain all the information needed to fit the cell-level model, so numerical optimization runs over donors rather than individual cells. In simulations and real-data evaluations, Fast-TWiST was more than 10 times faster than TWiST while matching its statistical performance. Applying the method to the OneK1K data, we identified 3,092 dynamic gene-disease associations that depend on biologically interpretable gene programs, including cytotoxicity, immediate early gene (IEG), BCL2/FAM13A, T helper 1-like (Th1-Like), and resting T helper 2 (Th2-Resting). Independent eQTL datasets and single-cell multiome data supported cell-state-specific regulatory effects that may be driving these findings.

papers.title: Optimizing Exomiser to prioritize candidate genes underlying monogenic forms of common disease
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe majority of rare diseases are caused by pathogenic variants in a single gene with Mendelian inheritance. In contrast, common diseases typically have complex genetic etiology, ranging from a cumulative impact of many common genetic variants with small individual effects, to fewer rare variants with larger effects, with monogenic forms at the rare end of the spectrum. While unknown prevalence of the monogenic fraction of common diseases and incomplete penetrance make identification of such monogenic forms of common diseases particularly challenging, their diagnosis can be essential for precision medicine. Automated rare variant prioritization tools, such as Exomiser, aid whole exome sequencing-based rare genetic disease diagnostics. However, Exomisers utility has not been systematically assessed in the context of monogenic forms of common diseases prior to this study. MethodsWe evaluated and optimized Exomiser for prioritization of rare pathogenic variants in common disease using a large kidney stone disease (KSD) cohort (701 cases, 200 controls). First, we benchmarked Exomisers performance across different settings for KSD "gold standard" variants in established KSD genes with Mendelian inheritance. Next, we utilized the optimal pipeline for discovery of novel KSD genes and compared Exomisers findings with results from gene-level rare variant enrichment analyses in an extended in-house cohort and the UK Biobank. ResultsWith the optimal approach, Exomiser ranked within the top five rankings nearly all (94%, N = 48) previously defined "gold standard" KSD gene-participant pairs from an established KSD gene panel. Using this tool, we additionally nominated 62 novel genes predominantly involved in ion homeostasis, which are now available to the scientific community as candidate genes for KSD. Out of these genes, orthogonal approaches also support ABCC6 as a strong KSD risk gene, in line with previous research, providing a proof-of-principle supporting the utility of Exomiser in the context of common disease. ConclusionsThis study serves as an example for automated variant prioritization in the context of monogenic forms of common diseases, which is a key step for precision medicine.

papers.title: Exome sequencing in individuals with oculoauriculofrontonasal syndrome provides further evidence of a non-traditional inheritance model
papers.abstract: The oculoauriculofrontonasal syndrome is a rare condition characterized by ocular hypertelorism, broad nose, mandibular hypoplasia, preauricular tags, and ear anomalies. Despite presenting a clinically recognizable pattern defined by the overlap of craniofacial microsomia and frontonasal dysplasia, its etiology remains unknown. Males and females are equally affected, and there is no recurrence reported. Genetic investigations performed to date could not clarify this issue yet. To further investigate Mendelian inheritance and test the hypothesis of a possible monogenic cause, we performed exome sequencing in a case series of Brazilian individuals from a single center with the clinical diagnosis of oculoauriculofrontonasal syndrome, including both solo and trio-based exome sequencing. The results provided here further support a non-traditional inheritance model, requiring additional studies including multi-omics approaches to elucidate its etiology.

papers.title: Transcriptional aging across CNS tissues in the ALS-FTD spectrum reflects clock architecture and disease-associated cellular signatures
papers.abstract: BackgroundWe examined transcriptomic (gene expression-based) aging in postmortem central nervous system (CNS) tissues from donors across the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)-frontotemporal dementia (FTD) spectrum and investigated the molecular and cellular features underlying disease-associated differences in transcriptional aging clocks. MethodsSix transcriptomic clocks (RNAAgeCalc DESeq2, GTExAge, Pearson and GenAge; Pasta REG and age-shift) were applied to 2,235 RNA-sequencing samples from 609 donors across 11 CNS regions, with adjustment for age and tissue-specific technical variables. We compared transcriptional age across ALS, ALS-FTD, FTD, and controls, examining regional variation, gene-level contributions, cell composition, disease duration, and C9orf72 status, with independent validation of gene contributions in a cervical spinal cord cohort. ResultsDisease-associated differences in transcriptional age varied by diagnosis, tissue, and clock. ALS and ALS-FTD showed the strongest differences in spinal cord, while FTD differences localized primarily to the frontal and temporal cortex. In ALS spinal cord, RNAAgeCalc DESeq2 estimates were lower than controls, whereas other clocks estimated higher transcriptional age when significant. CHIT1 was identified as the primary contributor to the DESeq2 transcriptional age decrease in ALS. Cell composition adjustment attenuated ALS spinal cord differences, reflecting microglial, lymphocyte, oligodendrocyte, and astrocyte signatures, though the lumbar GenAge increase in transcriptional age and DESeq2 decrease remained significant. The higher transcriptional age in ALS motor cortex also remained significantafter adjustment. Clinical associations were likewise clock dependent. Higher spinal DESeq2 age acceleration (AA) was associated with longer ALS duration, though this association was strongly influenced by the CHIT1 term. Higher GTExAge AA in cervical spinal cord, thoracic spinal cord, and occipital cortex was associated with shorter disease duration; no significant associations were observed for the other clock-tissue combinations or for ALS-FTD. No clock differed by C9orf72 repeat expansion status. ConclusionsIn this study we found disease-associated differences in transcriptional age that localize to clinically relevant tissues. Differences in transcriptional aging across the ALS-FTD spectrum reflect interactions among clock architecture, disease-associated gene expression, tissue region, and cellular composition. Resolving these components reveals the biological context underlying divergent clock estimates and provides a framework for interpreting changes in transcriptional aging.

papers.title: Escape from X-chromosome inactivation increases disease risk and drives sex-differential genetic effects: a population-scale PheXWAS
papers.abstract: X chromosome (Xchr) contribution to complex traits remains incomplete, due to its unique inheritance pattern and its inactivation mechanism. Therefore, we gathered data from 800,000 individuals from the UK Biobank and dbGaP, and performed a sex-stratified phenome-wide association study of Xchr variation across 3,741 complex traits. Heritability analyses revealed sex-specific patterns and an overall involvement of Xchr in complex phenotypes. We identified 6,531 loci significantly associated with 402 complex traits, with a higher proportion of associations consistent with dominant inheritance than observed for autosomes. Although effect directions were largely concordant between sexes, loci with significant effect-size differences were enriched for escape-gene associations. Escape genes were depleted among trait-associated loci and strongly enriched for risky disease effects. These association patterns enabled prediction of escape status for unannotated genes. This overview of Xchr contribution to complex traits suggests inactivation escape as a clear risky feature for females.

papers.title: Quantification of Bias-Variance Tradeoffs in Genome-Wide Polygenic Indices: When 'Good' PGIs are Bad and 'Bad' PGIs are Good
papers.abstract: Polygenic indices (PGIs) are downwardly biased in their predictive accuracies in independent samples due to the presence of estimation error in Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) from which they are constructed. By performing GWAS of the same phenotype in independent samples, we obtain to error-corrected estimates of PGI prediction accuracy, which we use to estimate the extent to which different PGI construction methods (unadjusted, Clumping, LDpred2-inf, LDpred2-auto, SBayesR, PRS-CS-auto) index total single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) heritability. To ensure practicality of this approach when individual-level data from the original GWAS are not available, we provide a means of synthetically splitting existing GWAS summary statistics into independent halves. In both simulated and empirical data, we find that advanced PGI construction methods that produce enhanced uncorrected prediction accuracies (often by shrinking individual SNP effects towards zero or exactly to zero) also produce deflated error-corrected prediction accuracies. LDpred2-inf, which most closely resembles a multiple regression estimator to account for linkage disequilibrium without further aggressive shrinkage, consistently produces PGIs with relatively lower uncorrected prediction accuracies but higher error-corrected prediction accuracies that nearly fully recover SNP heritability. We show that PGI construction methods that implement aggressive shrinkage may also provide biased patterns of associations with collateral phenotypes, irrespective of error correction. By providing a means of straightforwardly obtaining error-corrected estimates of prediction accuracy using PGIs derived from standard GWAS summary statistics, we have highlighted an uncommonly recognized bias-variance tradeoff associated with the choice of PGI construction methods.

papers.title: Evaluation of a Brief Educational Intervention to Improve Healthcare Provider Communication About Autism Genetic Testing
papers.abstract: Although professional guidelines recommend offering genetic testing following an autism diagnosis, uptake remains low in the United States. Healthcare providers frequently report limited education and uncertainty discussing autism genetics with patients and families. We developed and evaluated a brief educational intervention to improve provider communication about autism genetic testing, consisting of animated videos addressing autism genetics, available testing options, and strategies for discussing testing with autistic individuals and families. We evaluated the intervention among 100 U.S.-based healthcare providers and a community panel of 99 autistic adults. Participants completed a validated measure of genetic literacy before viewing the videos, then evaluated the intervention and its perceived impact on genetic testing. Providers showed higher genetic literacy than the general U.S. population, yet only 23% reported frequently discussing genetic testing before the intervention. Afterward, 86% reported greater likelihood of recommending genetic testing following diagnosis, and 88% reported the videos changed how they would discuss genetics with patients and families. Both cohorts rated the resources favorably, and 71% of autistic adults reported greater likelihood of pursuing genetic testing after viewing the videos. Brief, communication-focused educational resources may improve workflows for autism genetic testing and support informed decision-making for providers, autistic individuals, and their families.

papers.title: One blood methylation profile stratifies ten-year risk across 21 common diseases
papers.abstract: Blood DNA methylation offers a dynamic readout of inherited and acquired influences on health, creating an opportunity for risk prediction beyond polygenic scores, which are fixed at conception and have yet to demonstrate broad clinical utility. As such, we aimed to develop methylation risk scores for 21 common diseases in 12,785 adults from Generation Scotland and the Mass General Brigham Biobank, combining technically reproducible probes, null-calibrated feature selection and ten-year survival models, with evaluation in a single holdout that was not used for feature selection, model fitting or tuning. The methylation risk scores for eight diseases reached a holdout C-index of at least 0.80: chronic kidney disease, peripheral vascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart failure and type 2 diabetes with at least 50 events each, and interstitial lung disease, dementia and fatty liver disease with fewer. For the five scores with at least 50 events, adjusted hazard ratios per standard deviation ranged from 2.6 to 4.1, with the highest risk tertile containing 73 to 90% of the ten-year events. Panel CpGs were enriched for cytokine signalling, innate immune sensing and sterol metabolism. Against reported values, the eight top-tier methylation risk scores exceed published polygenic and methylation scores alone, and exceed published polygenic and methylation scores that include clinical covariates for seven of the eight diseases (the exception is type 2 diabetes, where our AUC of 0.865 without clinical risk factors is close to a methylation-plus-risk-factor model at 0.872, and our C-index of 0.809 is lower than the C-index for a polygenic-plus-risk-factor at 0.85). These results indicate that a single blood methylation profile can rank ten-year risk for several common diseases at a level that compares favourably with published genetic and methylation scores.

papers.title: Rare copy number variation in alcohol use disorder using whole-genome sequencing in the All of Us Research Program
papers.abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is common, heritable (h2 [~]50%) and polygenic, but the contribution of rare structural variation is largely unexamined. Using short-read whole-genome sequencing (srWGS) data from the All of Us Research Program, we tested the association of rare copy number variants (rCNV; minor allele frequency <1%) with AUD in 56,062 participants (5,410 cases, 50,652 controls) defined from electronic health records. Analyses were conducted within European-like (EUR; N=29,392), African-like (AFR; N=8,269) and Admixed American-like (AMR; N=8,049) samples and combined by cross-ancestry meta-analysis. We tested genome-wide rCNV burden, burden within AUD-related, mouse behavioral and neuropsychiatric gene sets, and individual rCNV regions. No genome-wide burden metric or individual rCNV region [≥]10 kb was associated with AUD after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Significant gene-set results were almost exclusively duplications associated with reduced AUD risk across biologically unrelated sets, suggesting a global duplication dosage effect rather than pathway-specific enrichment. In contrast, deletion count within a Neurof_UnionStringent (Neurofunction Union Stringent) gene set was associated with increased AUD risk (OR=1.04, FDR=0.044), and deletions in xenobiotic-response genes showed nominal associations in multiple ancestry groups. Among rCNV of all sizes, a 58 bp deletion at 16p12.1, a dosage-sensitive neuropsychiatric locus, was significant in the cross-ancestry analysis (OR=2.93, FDR=0.030) without significant heterogeneity. rCNV detectable by srWGS do not appear to contribute substantially to AUD liability at current sample sizes.

papers.title: Brain Cell-Type-Specific X-Chromosome Gene Regulation Reveals Sex-Biased Candidate Genes in Neurodegeneration
papers.abstract: The impact of X-chromosome dosage on gene regulation in specific brain cell-types may importantly shape sex differences in neurodegenerative diseases but remains poorly resolved. We therefore mapped X-chromosome genetic effects on gene expression, i.e. cis-expression quantitative trait loci (cis-eQTL), across seven brain cell-types from 423 old-age individuals. We identified 212 X-linked genes whose expression was genetically regulated, with the majority being cell-type specific. Notably, 10 of these genes ([~]5%) showed sex-heterogeneous genetic regulation. Through sex-differential expression analyses we further discovered 101 sex-biased genes that were predominantly female-upregulated most strikingly in microglia. Sex-biased gene expression showed both shared and distinct cell-type effects, appearing most divergent in non-neuronal populations. Many female-biased genes overlapped known escape-from-X-inactivation genes and were enriched for links to Alzheimers disease. Finally, we integrated our resource with X-chromosome-wide association studies of neurodegenerative diseases through causal inference approaches including transcriptome-wide association, mendelian randomization, and colocalization analyses to nominate 11 candidate causal genes, linked to their respective cell-types and sex-informed mechanisms, for Alzheimers disease, Parkinsons disease, and Multiple System Atrophy. Altogether, our findings suggest escape from X chromosome inactivation may contribute to sex differences in neurodegeneration and provide a resource to advance sex-informed insights into disease pathogenesis and therapeutic opportunities.

papers.title: Plasma Proteogenomic Uncovers Novel Molecular Mechanisms of Soluble Endoglin and Identifies AZI2 as a new Player in Arteriovenous Malformations in Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia
papers.abstract: Endoglin is a transmembrane glycoprotein that plays a key role in vascular development, angiogenesis and endothelial homeostasis. Its soluble form (Sol-ENG), generated through proteolytic shedding of the membrane-bound protein, has been implicated in the pathophysiology of numerous cardiovascular diseases, ranging from common conditions such as preeclampsia and thrombosis to rare diseases such as hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT). Leveraging large-scale genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics data from public and original resources, we identify a molecular signature of 24 markers associated with plasma levels of Sol-ENG. This signature was enriched in genes coding for GPI-enchored proteins and included metabolites participating to glycosylation and redox homeostasis. Furthermore, we observed that ABO blood groups and genetically predicted plasma levels of 5-Azacytidine Induced 2 (AZI2) associate with the risk of arteriovenous malformations in HHT patients. This study provides new insights into the physiological mechanisms underlying Endoglin regulation and opens clinical perspectives for the management of HHT patients.

papers.title: Promoter methylation of LDLR is not a common cause of familial hypercholesterolemia
papers.abstract: Background/ObjectivesFamilial hypercholesterolemia (FH) is a widely prevalent inherited disorder defined by chronically high LDL-C concentrations and a significantly increased risk of cardiovascular disease. While FH is primarily an autosomal dominant disease caused by pathogenic mutations in LDLR, APOB, or PCSK9, approximately 20-60% of clinically diagnosed patients are mutation-negative. A previous survey of over 23,000 methylation profiles identified a differentially methylated region in the promoter of LDLR. This study aimed to investigate whether constitutional hypermethylation of the LDLR promoter is a recurrent cause of FH in patients lacking identifiable pathogenic variants. MethodsWe screened 308 mutation-negative clinically confirmed FH patients for promoter hypermethylation in LDLR. We used Combined Bisulfite Restriction Analysis (COBRA) with genomic DNA from peripheral blood samples. The assay assessed methylation at TaqI sites within a 332 bp region of the LDLR promoter. ResultsNo instances of LDLR promoter hypermethylation were detected among the 308 mutation-negative FH patients. Statistical analysis yielded an upper bound of 1.19% (95% Clopper-Pearson CI) for the prevalence of this specific epimutation in our cohort. ConclusionsOur results indicate that LDLR promoter hypermethylation at this specific locus is not a common cause of the FH phenotype in mutation-negative patients. These findings imply that while methylation in this region may be rare or not significantly contribute to the disease phenotype, the diagnostic gap in FH may be explained by other factors, such as methylation in other regions, polygenic risk, structural variants, or non-canonical regulatory mutations.

papers.title: Circulating immune architecture across age, exposures and disease in ethnically diverse UK cohorts.
papers.abstract: Human immune composition reflects genetic background and cumulative life-course exposures, yet how these influences shape immune architecture across populations and disease remains poorly understood. Here we integrate single-cell transcriptomics, matched clinical haematology and electronic health records from 5,079 individuals of European, British-Pakistani and British-Bangladeshi ancestries to quantify 26 circulating immune cell types and 62 transcriptional states. We map immune compositional variation associated with age, sex, adiposity and smoking, revealing distinct patterns across adulthood and associations between modifiable exposures and advanced immune age. Across common diseases, immune compositional signatures converge on recurrent inflammatory myeloid, adaptive-memory and interferon programmes, whose expression varies with age and population context. Cardiovascular therapies are associated with selective shifts in disease-associated immune states. Immune composition further discriminates common cardiometabolic diseases and resolves patients into endotypes with distinct metabolic and clinical profiles. These findings establish circulating immune architecture as an integrative phenotype linking life-course exposures, population context and disease, providing a framework for precision population immunology.

papers.title: Hierarchical genetic regulatory architecture of the human immune system informs complex disease mechanisms
papers.abstract: How inherited genetic variation propagates through multicellular regulatory systems to influence human disease remains poorly understood. To reconstruct the regulatory architecture of genetic variation on circulating immune cells, we analysed single-cell transcriptomes from 6.7 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 4,452 European-ancestry UK Biobank participants, identifying 114,063 independent cis-regulatory effects affecting 15,419 genes. Using a new statistical workflow (FLANDERS), we map the hierarchical organisation of these effects and the underlying regulatory architecture across tissues, immune lineages, cell types and cell states. We find that disease-associated variants predominantly act through regulatory programmes shared within immune lineages and broad cellular compartments, rather than through highly specific cellular states. We show that local cis-regulatory effects commonly act through coherent regulatory pathways implicating transcription factor cascades and intercellular signalling, which allows linking together multiple disease genes. We demonstrate independent support for these genes and mechanisms through rare variant associations. Our findings reveal a highly organised structure of immune regulatory variation shaping human disease, and provide a highly effective framework for interpreting disease associations and prioritising therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Additional value of germline genomic scores beyond prostate-specific antigen alone for long-term and near-term prostate cancer risk
papers.abstract: We evaluated whether germline genomic risk complements prostate-specific antigen (PSA) for prostate cancer early detection. P-CARE integrates a 601-variant polygenic hazard score, family history, and genetic ancestry. Long-term outcomes and clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) detection on biopsy were assessed in the Million Veteran Program (MVP), with external validation in the Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial (PCPT). Among 428,512 MVP participants, high versus low P-CARE risk was associated with increased hazards of treatment (HR 3.32) and metastasis (HR 3.32). Among men whose baseline PSA was measured at ages 40-49 with PSA 1-3 ng/mL, 15-year treatment/metastasis probabilities were 2.6%, 4.5%, and 10.2% across increasing P-CARE risk groups. High P-CARE risk also predicted csPCa on biopsy (OR 2.96), while PRSPSA was inversely associated with outcomes. Findings were consistent in PCPT. Germline genomic risk complements measured PSA, supporting prospective evaluation of genetically informed screening strategies.

papers.title: MRCAT: A multi-agent framework for reliable Mendelian randomization analysis and causal interpretation
papers.abstract: Mendelian randomization (MR) uses genetic variants to estimate causal effects of exposures on health outcomes, but rigorous MR analyses require coordinated procedures and interpretation under explicit methodological assumptions. Although artificial intelligence (AI) agents can automate analyses, computational completion does not guarantee scientific reliability. Here, we present MRCAT, a multi-agent framework that translates MR-specific knowledge into an AI-assisted workflow that is plannable, executable, verifiable, recoverable and traceable. MRCAT combines dependency-aware planning, Skill-guided execution and expertinformed review with traceable reporting guided by STROBE-MR, a guideline for clear and transparent reporting of MR studies, and iterative Writer-Judge checking. We evaluated MRCAT on 30 natural-language queries spanning diverse data sources, analytical requirements and boundary conditions. MRCAT achieved scientific completion, defined as meeting all nine prespecified MR-specific procedural requirements, for all 26 executable queries and appropriately handled all four boundary cases, compared with 17, 11 and 4 scientifically completed queries for Claude Code, Biomni and BioMedAgent, respectively. Across six independently curated tasks for which the expert-curated analyses did not support causal effects, MRCAT showed closer numerical concordance with the expert-curated analyses and produced interpretations consistent with expertcurated conclusions in all six cases, compared with two for Claude Code and four for Biomni. Additional case studies demonstrated evidence-grounded reporting and selective reuse of analytical outputs in multi-exposure and bidirectional MR investigations. MRCAT provides a framework for reducing the operational burden of MR research while supporting reproducible analysis, assumption-consistent interpretation and traceable scientific reporting.

papers.title: Multimodal population-scale cell atlases define archetypes and extremes of human blood
papers.abstract: The cellular composition of blood is fundamental to human physiology and is routinely measured to assess health and disease. Circulating immune cells show extensive heterogeneity, but the organising principles and extremes of variation across individuals remain undefined. Here, using single-cell transcriptomics across two biobank cohorts encompassing [~]6,000 individuals, we show that human blood occupies recurrent archetypal states defined by coordinated cell composition patterns. We delineate three major archetypes spanning naive lymphoid, myeloid and cytotoxic composition, and two minor archetypes characterised by type I interferon-driven inflammation and expanded premalignant CD5+ B cells. We develop cell2clone to infer lymphocyte clonal expansions, revealing how reactive clonal processes drive the cytotoxic archetype and premalignant clonal expansion establishes the CD5+ B cell archetype, creating outlier states that uncover context-specific effects of germline variants. Clonal haematopoiesis and mosaic chromosomal alterations influence blood states in an archetype-dependent manner. The archetype framework links blood states to common disease risk and clinical blood counts and, through a machine-learning model ArcheTypist, classifies infection and cancer immunotherapy outcomes. This population-scale framework has implications for diagnostics, early disease detection, immunotherapy stratification and mechanistic insights into disease susceptibility and therapy response, providing an organising model for identifying compositional subtypes across human tissues.

papers.title: Integrative Multi-Ancestry and Multi-Tissue Fine-Mapping Prioritizes Candidate Causal Genes for Risk of Breast Cancer and Its Subtypes
papers.abstract: Most breast cancer (BC) risk loci identified by genome-wide association studies lie in noncoding regions, and traditional transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) often prioritize multiple correlated genes per locus. We applied two gene fine-mapping methods, TGVIS and M-cTWAS, which jointly model gene expression, splicing and alternative polyadenylation (APA) with direct variant effects, to overall BC, estrogen receptor-negative (ER-negative) BC and triple-negative BC (TNBC) in women of European and African ancestry. Using 11 BC-relevant GTEx v10 tissues, we prioritized 31, 13 and 5 candidate causal genes, respectively, in European-ancestry populations. Compared with marginal TWAS, fine-mapping reduced the number of candidate genes per locus by 72-88%, and credible sets explained 97- 100% of significant marginal associations. Seven candidates were not reported by previous GTEx v8-based TWAS, including RIN3, supported only by APA, and NPAT for TNBC. Analyses across 48 tissues and brain cell types revealed brain contributions, including ARHGEF5 in oligodendrocytes. In African-ancestry populations, EN1 was prioritized for ER-negative BC and TNBC through variants common in African but rare in European ancestry. These results refine BC susceptibility genes, highlight regulatory mechanisms beyond breast tissue and gene expression, and reveal the challenge of mapping GWAS variants to causal genes with currently available data.

papers.title: Complementary DNA-contact and domain-destabilizing mechanisms of PAX9 and MSX1 variants in non-syndromic tooth agenesis: an AlphaFold 3, ThermoMPNN, and AlphaGenome study
papers.abstract: Missense variants in the DNA-binding domains of PAX9 and MSX1 cause non-syndromic tooth agenesis, yet most substitutions remain variants of uncertain significance. We investigated the structural mechanisms of 39 pathogenic missense variants in the PAX9 paired domain (n = 32) and MSX1 homeodomain (n = 7) alongside 77 non-coding/splice ClinVar variants. We modelled protein-DNA complexes with AlphaFold 3, estimated folding stability changes ({Delta}{Delta}G) with ThermoMPNN, and compared pathogenic variants with gnomAD v4 domain variants. AlphaFold 3 confidence metrics and mutant interfaces were insensitive to point mutations. Instead, pathogenic PAX9 variants acted through two complementary mechanisms relative to recurrent population controls: loss of direct DNA contact ( 0.564) showed 8%-21% specificity across both domains. Mechanism did not predict missing teeth, whereas missense variants were milder than null alleles (p = 0.001). AlphaGenome matched SpliceAI and jointly prioritized seven intronic variants.

papers.title: Excess of de novo substitutions in the genomes of individuals with newly acquired germline TP53 mutations
papers.abstract: Inherited defects in the tumour suppressor gene TP53 cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome, a highly penetrant predisposition to childhood and adult cancers. About half of affected individuals carry a variant absent from both parents, and these are the patients missed by family-history-based testing criteria. Where and when such variants arise, in which parental gamete or after fertilisation, remains unresolved, as primary family data are scarce. We addressed this using whole-genome and linked-read sequencing of five family quartets, each comprising a proband with a confirmed newly arisen pathogenic TP53 variant, a closely age-matched unaffected sibling, and both parents, drawn from a cohort of 429 families meeting clinical criteria for the syndrome; matching for age controls for the strong dependence of mutation counts on parental age. Every proband carried a distinct heterozygous missense change in the DNA-binding domain of p53, and read-based phasing traced four of five to the paternal chromosome. Genome-wide, probands carried a significant excess of newly arisen single-nucleotide changes relative to their siblings, which persisted after correction for parental age and was detected on the paternal chromosome. No comparable excess was found for insertions, deletions, structural rearrangements or repeat expansions, and the excess mutations matched the two clock-like processes operating in all cells rather than any distinct mechanism. These features are hard to reconcile with an event confined to the parental germ cells, and instead point to TP53 variants that arise shortly after fertilisation and sweep the embryo, carrying neighbouring mutations with them. Consistent with such sweeps occurring throughout life, clonal TP53 mutations in two large public tumour-genome collections ranked above other clonal driver mutations in cancer cell fraction within tumours, as expected when a cancer emerges within a pre-existing mutant patch of normal tissue. We propose that constitutional TP53 variants and these mutant patches form one continuum, distinguished principally by timing: a sweep during the first cleavage divisions produces a variant present throughout the body, whereas the same advantage acting later confines the clone to one tissue. This would reframe a subset of Li-Fraumeni syndrome as an early developmental rather than strictly germline event, with implications for testing, counselling and surveillance.

papers.title: A new liability-based rare-variant burden test identifies a novel genetic association between HTRA3 and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
papers.abstract: In contrast to large-effect monogenic variants, which are highly penetrant regardless of genetic background, variants with more modest effect sizes depend on a carriers genetic background to manifest disease. For many complex traits, including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), polygenic risk scores (PRS) have been shown to capture a significant proportion of the genetic background risk. While a rare-variant association test incorporating a PRS covariate to account for the genetic background has been demonstrated to improve statistical power for gene discovery in quantitative traits, for binary traits, this approach shows limited or no power gain over PRS-unadjusted tests. Here, we propose a novel rare-variant association test for binary traits that jointly models the contribution of rare variants and PRS under a liability threshold model. In simulated datasets, our new method, liability threshold burden test (LTBT), shows a well-controlled false positive rate and outperforms the sensitivity of existing methods. To demonstrate this new method, we apply it to sequencing datasets for IPF, a rare but highly morbid lung disease. By accounting for an individuals genetic background with PRS, we identify and formally replicate a significant novel association of rare predicted damaging missense variants in HTRA3 (HtrA serine peptidase 3) with IPF.

papers.title: Combined genome-wide association studies in humans and cattle: Cross-species genetic insights into dizygotic twinning
papers.abstract: To leverage independent genetic evidence from multiple species, we developed a cross-species gene-based GWAS meta-analysis framework and applied this to Dizygotic Twinning (DZT) in humans and cattle. After meta-analysis within species, we converted human and cattle GWAS summary statistics to gene-level association signals within each species, mapped genes across species through human-cattle orthology, and then combined gene-level evidence for orthologous genes across the two species. DZT is defined as giving birth to multiple offspring after a single pregnancy resulting from spontaneous multiple ovulation. In humans, DZT occurs in about 1% of pregnancies with heritability estimates of 20% to 30% whilst in cattle DZT occurs in 1-5% of pregnancies and heritability is estimated at about 11%. Here, we present the largest human GWAS meta-analysis including data from 1,395,285 participants. We identified 16 genetic regions of interest, including 12 independent loci from the SNP based analyses and 4 genes identified in the gene-based MAGMA analyses. Among the prioritized genes are follicle stimulation hormone receptor (FSHR) and growth differentiation factor 9 (GDF9), that both are involved in ovarian folliculogenesis. Cattle GWAS summary statistics were based on data from 2,656 Irish Holstein bulls with estimated breeding values for predisposition to twinning based on 2,238,936 birth records, and 86,391 German Holstein dams. After combining the gene-level analyses for 13,225 genes mapped as orthologous across the human and cattle data we identify FSHR as a central locus for DZT in both humans and cattle. We find evidence of additional associations, including ACVR2A, which plays a role in embryonic implantation and TUFM, which has previously been implicated in premature ovarian insufficiency. Our approach provides a promising framework for future cross-species comparative GWAS studies. It shows benefits for gene discovery and gene prioritization and in our application expands available functional follow-up data, allowing us to leverage cattle eQTL data to resolve human GWAS loci. The method and underlying philosophy presented here are transferable to other shared phenotypes across several species.

papers.title: Mapping Gene-by-Environment Interactions via the Plasma Exposome at Cell-Type Resolution
papers.abstract: Gene-by-environment (GxE) interactions inform where genetics and environment converge to impact human health and disease. However, systematically mapping GxE interactions has been challenging due to the diversity of testable exposures and a lack of scalable approaches to measure the environments cells experience in vivo. Here, we identified modules of correlated plasma metabolites and proteins and used them as quantitative proxies for environmental exposures experienced by circulating leukocytes. We demonstrated that these proxies are associated with environmentally-modifiable clinical traits such as diet and infection and support broad mapping of gene-by-environment (G x E) interactions affecting gene expression and CpG methylation in leukocytes. We identified significant interactions for 95.2% of tested genes and 5.9% of tested methylation sites. These G x E interactions showed specificity to exposures and cell type. Colocalization analysis further provided links between interactions and complex trait and disease loci. Finally, we expanded G x E interaction mapping to unexplored cell types using a zero-shot transfer model to predict GxE interactions in held-out cell types, demonstrating how plasma metabolomics and proteomics can enhance the discovery of G x E interactions across the body. Altogether, this work provides a systematic multi-omic framework to study how gene regulation is shaped by both the genome and the molecular environments cells experience in vivo.
